title: When the House Turns
premise: Tamsin Blackwood returns to the family house to bury her twin sister, only to learn the body in the casket is wearing her face—and the excavation crew digging the new foundation unearths a door sealed from the inside, with scratch marks on the wrong side. As night falls, Tamsin realizes the house has been keeping a ledger of everyone who was ever 'invited in,' and that her sister made a bargain to trade places with her. To survive until sunrise, she must uncover what her grandmother signed over decades ago and decide whether to honor the contract, destroy it, or sign it herself—ending with Tamsin burning the deed in the hearth as the door opens at dawn, freeing whatever was kept, while she walks out of a house that finally forgets her name.
about_author: Ines Oyelaran is a former probate clerk from coastal Maine who spent years cataloguing deeds to houses that no longer appear on any map. She writes horror about inheritance, paperwork, and the things families agree to without reading the fine print.

chapters.title: The Wrong Face in the Casket
chapters.summary: POV: Tamsin. At the wake, Tamsin stares into the open casket and sees her own face on the corpse of her twin, Sable—down to a scar she alone should have. Relatives murmur that grief plays tricks. The emotional beat: uncanny dread masked by funeral politeness, as Tamsin begins doubting which twin actually died.

chapters.title: Counted Doors
chapters.summary: POV: Tamsin. Settling into the house for the estate settlement, Tamsin counts eleven doors though the blueprints show ten, and finds fresh chalk tally marks behind the pantry. Her aunt Verna warns her never to answer knocking after dark. The beat: creeping domestic wrongness; the house is watching how she moves through it.

chapters.title: What the Excavator Found
chapters.summary: POV: Dev, the crew foreman. Digging the new foundation, Dev's crew strikes not stone but a door—oak, iron-banded, hinged on the inside, scratched raw from within. The foreman's radio dies mid-sentence when he describes it aloud. The beat: awe curdling into fear; something was locked away by people who meant it.

chapters.title: The Ledger in the Walls
chapters.summary: POV: Tamsin. Searching her grandmother's study, Tamsin finds a ledger listing every person ever 'invited in' to the house across four generations—each name paired with a date and a debt. Sable's name appears twice: once as invited, once as payment. The beat: horrified clarity; the family fortune was collateral.

chapters.title: Verna's Confession
chapters.summary: POV: Verna. In flashbacks braided with the present, Verna admits she witnessed the original signing: their grandmother traded a child's future for the house's protection during a desperate winter, and the 'last resident' must always renew the papers. The beat: guilt and complicity; justice was never legal here, only contractual.

chapters.title: Knocking
chapters.summary: POV: Tamsin. Night one of the holdout: knocking circles the house, testing every door, speaking in Sable's voice, then Tamsin's own. Dev arrives seeking shelter after his crew abandons the site. The beat: siege terror; invisibility—the survival strategy of ignored daughters—no longer works.

chapters.title: The Papers on the Table
chapters.summary: POV: Tamsin. At midnight the study fills with the smell of ink and the deed rewrites itself, offering renewal in exchange for 'one twin, freely given.' Tamsin realizes Sable forged her signature years ago and fled; the casket held a substitute the house rejected. The beat: betrayal and rage; her sister tried to sell her.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: POV: Dev. Dev discovers the door's scratches form words—a previous resident's warning that the contract voids only if the deed burns before dawn and no one signs. But the fire must be lit by someone named in the ledger, and Verna refuses, insisting the debt protects them all. The beat: desperate hope against inherited cowardice.

chapters.title: The Last Resident Signs
chapters.summary: POV: Tamsin. Climax. Verna signs the papers to save herself, and the eleventh door opens, releasing what the house kept fed. Tamsin wrests the deed away, drags it to the hearth as the thing wearing Sable's face offers her everything she was ever denied—recognition, inheritance, love. The beat: the choice between being seen and being free.

chapters.title: A House That Forgets
chapters.summary: POV: Tamsin. Dawn. The deed burns; the door stands open on empty earth; the ledger's names fade to blank pages. Verna, aged overnight, leaves without a word. Tamsin walks out past Dev, and the house's windows go dark one by one, forgetting her. The beat: bittersweet release—justice outside the law costs the inheritance itself, and she pays it gladly.
